details:
**The Temple of the Golden Pavilion**
Mishima's 1956 novel, based on the real 1950 burning of Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto. The narrator Mizoguchi, an ugly, stuttering acolyte trained at the temple under its superior, Father Dosen, becomes obsessed with the temple's beauty and comes to feel he must destroy it. Near the end of the war he wishes "let the darkness of my heart equal the darkness of the night." After setting the fire, he throws away the arsenic and knife he brought to kill himself, smokes a cigarette, and decides that he wants to live.

**"When you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha"**
A Zen saying from the Rinzai Roku (the recorded sayings of the master Linji) that Mizoguchi remembers just before he sets fire to the Golden Pavilion. He takes it as permission to destroy what he worships.

**Kashiwagi**
Mizoguchi's cynical, clubfooted friend at Otani University, who boasts that he uses his deformity to seduce women by making them pity him. Kashiwagi and Mizoguchi discuss the Zen koan "Nansen kills a kitten," which Father Dosen tells the acolytes from The Gateless Gate, a collection of koans; in the koan, Joshu responds by putting his sandals on his head.

**Confessions of a Mask**
Mishima's semi-autobiographical 1949 novel about Kochan, a young man who hides his homosexuality behind a "mask" of normality. It opens with Kochan claiming to remember the moment of his own birth, which disturbs the adults around him. As a schoolboy he is drawn to the physique of the older classmate Omi.

**Joan of Arc and Saint Sebastian**
Two images from Kochan's childhood in Confessions of a Mask. He is disgusted when his nurse tells him that a picture of a handsome knight he loves actually shows Joan of Arc, a woman. Later, Guido Reni's painting of the martyred Saint Sebastian gives him his first sexual arousal, feeding his obsession with beautiful young men dying.

**Sonoko**
The sister of Kochan's friend Kusano in Confessions of a Mask, whose piano playing captivated him. He tries to fall in love with her but cannot feel desire for her. In the final scene, while he is with her, he is entranced by a shirtless young tough with a peony tattoo on his chest.

**The Sea of Fertility**
Mishima's final tetralogy, named after a lunar mare: Spring Snow, Runaway Horses, The Temple of Dawn, and The Decay of the Angel. It follows Shigekuni Honda, who goes from law student to judge to old man while trying to protect a series of reincarnations of his friend Kiyoaki Matsugae, an effort that ultimately ruins him.

**Spring Snow and Kiyoaki Matsugae**
The first Sea of Fertility novel, set among the aristocracy around 1912. Kiyoaki, a student at the Peers School, has a doomed love affair with Satoko Ayakura after she is engaged to an imperial prince. He dies young after giving Honda his dream diary and saying they will meet again "beneath the falls." Two Siamese princes at the school leave after one loses his emerald ring.

**Three moles and the reincarnations**
Honda recognizes Kiyoaki's reincarnations by a cluster of three moles on the left side of the body. The reincarnations are Isao Iinuma, a young kendo fanatic in Runaway Horses who plots to assassinate capitalist businessmen; the Thai princess Ying Chan in The Temple of Dawn; and the orphan Toru Yasunaga, whom the elderly Honda adopts in The Decay of the Angel.

**Seppuku in 1970**
On November 25, 1970, after delivering the final Sea of Fertility manuscript, Mishima and members of his private militia, the Tatenokai, took over a Self-Defense Forces headquarters in Tokyo and called for a coup to restore the emperor's power. When the soldiers jeered him, he committed ritual suicide by seppuku. His real name was Kimitake Hiraoka.

**The Sailor Who Fell from Grace with the Sea**
A 1963 novel about 13-year-old Noboru, who spies through a peephole on his widowed mother Fusako and her lover, the sailor Ryuji Tsukazaki. Noboru's gang of boys, led by a self-proclaimed "genius" called the chief, decides that Ryuji has betrayed his heroic calling by settling down, and they plan to kill him.

**The Sound of Waves**
A 1954 pastoral romance set on a small fishing island. The young fisherman Shinji wins the right to marry Hatsue, the daughter of a wealthy shipowner, by swimming through a typhoon to secure a ship to its mooring buoy. Translated by Meredith Weatherby, it was Mishima's first novel published in English.

**Sun and Steel**
Mishima's autobiographical essay about how, after a bookish youth, he turned to bodybuilding and martial arts to discover his own body and link words with action. It uses the image of an apple cut open to show its hidden core.

**Forbidden Colors**
A novel in which the aging writer Shunsuke Hinoki takes revenge on the women who wronged him by using Yuichi, a beautiful gay young man trapped in a sham marriage, to break their hearts. Mishima's widow objected to its use in Paul Schrader's film Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters, so it was left out.

**Thirst for Love**
An early Mishima novel influenced by François Mauriac. The widow Etsuko, living in her father-in-law's house, becomes obsessed with the young gardener Saburo, who is having an affair with the maid Miyo.
